newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ISMA chief sees no danger in new UK regulation.
newsitem.headline: ISMA chief sees no danger in new UK regulation.

text.p: The international securities industry is unlikely to be affected by the dramatic reforms planned for Britain's regulatory system, the chief executive of its main self-regulatory body said.

"We have no reason to think that they (the SIB) are unhappy with us in any shape or form," John Langton, chief executive of the International Securities Market Association (ISMA) told Reuters in an interview before the start of its annual general meeting on Thursday.
"We have no reason to believe that anything will be done to jeopardise our statutory position in the UK," he said.
Earlier this month, British finance minister Gordon Brown unveiled sweeping plans to overhaul regulation of Britain's financial services industry.

The Securities and Investment Board (SIB) will become one of the most powerful institutions, responsible for regulating all banks, securities firms and insurance companies. Self-Regulatory Organisations (SROs), of which ISMA is one, will become part of the SIB.
"The SIB is preparing a briefing for July. It remains to be seen whether there will be an abolition of SROs and whether regulation will get tougher," Langton said.

ISMA performs two roles, one as an SRO and another as an industry association for its 820 members in 48 countries. Its main role is to facilitate a self-regulatory framework for the continued growth and development of cross-border trading in international securities.

The introduction in 1989 of TRAX, a trade confirmation and risk management system, did much to alleviate SIB worries about risks in the securities industry at the time. Market volatility has made the need for such systems vital as a way of reducing sytemic risks in the industry.
"We have done a good job regarding trade reporting, and have provided what we were expected to do as an exchange," Langton said.

In 1988, the ISMA was appointed as a Designated Investment Exchange (DIE) by the SIB. It also got approval from the UK Treasury as the only International Self-Regulating Organisation (ISSRO) for the purposes of the 1986 UK Financial Services Act.
"(What the SIB will do) remains a question mark. We will wait and see, and monitor what happens," Langton said.
